header.title: Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP)
header.description: Build a linear model where some variables can be continuous, integer, or binary/Boolean. The feasible set is no longer only a convex polyhedron: integrality restricts admissible points to a discrete lattice, so the solver searches a branch-and-bound tree over LP relaxations.

import.info_body: A MILP JSON file extends the LP schema with variables[].integrality. Use C for continuous, I for integer, and B for binary/Boolean variables. Binary variables are normalized to bounds [0, 1]. Optional solver settings can include time_limit and mip_gap.

vars.hint: Choose the mathematical domain of each decision variable: continuous, integer, or binary.

solver.hint: MILP solve time can grow quickly. Use an optional time limit or relative MIP gap when a good incumbent is enough.
solver.info_body: Time limit stops the search after the given number of seconds. If the solver has an incumbent, status can be Feasible: the solution satisfies all constraints but is not proven optimal. MIP gap is the relative distance between the incumbent and the best bound; smaller values require stronger proof and can take longer.

header.title: Knapsack
header.description: Choose the knapsack variant, then describe items, capacities, and decision limits. The executable variants in this build are 0/1, Bounded, Unbounded, Fractional, and Multi-dimensional.

variant.hint: Select the mathematical meaning of each decision variable. Each variant changes the domain of x_i and therefore the structure of the solved model.

descriptions.zero_one: Each item can be selected once or excluded: x_i is binary.
descriptions.bounded: Each item can be selected an integer quantity up to a maximum limit: 0 <= x_i <= u_i.
descriptions.unbounded: Each item can be selected any non-negative integer quantity, limited only by capacity.
descriptions.fractional: A fraction of each item can be selected: x_i is continuous between 0 and 1.
descriptions.multi_dimensional: Each selected item consumes several resources at once, such as weight, volume, time, or budget.

placeholders.bounded: Each row adds a maximum quantity u_i. The solver chooses an integer quantity x_i between 0 and u_i to maximize total value within capacity.
placeholders.unbounded: Each row describes an item type that can be selected in any non-negative integer quantity, limited only by capacity.
placeholders.fractional: Each item can also be selected partially. The solver sorts by value/weight ratio and chooses fractions between 0 and 1.
placeholders.multi_dimensional: Each item consumes several resources: weight, volume, time, budget, or other capacities. The solver chooses a 0/1 subset that satisfies every limit.

import.json_tooltip: Import a Knapsack problem in Optees JSON format
import.json_info_body: The JSON file describes the problem variant, capacities, and items. Optees automatically selects the matching form panel.
import.json_info_html:
Main fields

Use version = 1, problem_type = knapsack, variant, and an items array. Accepted variants are zero_one, bounded, unbounded, fractional, and multi_dimensional.

Single resource

{
  "version": "1",
  "problem_type": "knapsack",
  "variant": "bounded",
  "capacity": 7,
  "items": [
    {"name": "A", "value": 6, "weight": 2, "max_quantity": 3},
    {"name": "B", "value": 10, "weight": 3, "max_quantity": 2}
  ]
}

Multi-dimensional

Add domain to specify the quantity domain: zero_one, bounded, unbounded, or fractional. Each item uses a usage vector with the same length as the resources array.

{
  "version": "1",
  "variant": "multi_dimensional",
  "domain": "fractional",
  "resources": [
    {"name": "weight", "capacity": 10},
    {"name": "volume", "capacity": 6}
  ],
  "items": [
    {"name": "A", "value": 8, "usage": [4, 1.5], "max_quantity": 1},
    {"name": "B", "value": 9, "usage": [5, 2], "max_quantity": "inf"}
  ]
}

Numeric rules

For 0/1, bounded, and unbounded, weight and capacity must be non-negative integers. In fractional mode, weight and capacity may be decimal numbers. Use inf in upper limits when the domain allows it.

capacity.label: Maximum capacity
capacity.info_body: Capacity is the maximum total weight that the selected items may use.
capacity.info_html:
Rule

The solver enforces sum weight_i x_i <= capacity.

Input

Capacity must be a non-negative integer because the current exact dynamic-programming algorithm indexes capacities from 0 to C.

Scale

The running time grows with number_of_items * capacity. Large capacities may require a MILP or another knapsack algorithm.

items.hint: Enter one row per item. Value can be decimal; weight and capacity must be non-negative integers.
items.fractional_hint: Enter one row per item. Value, weight, and capacity can be decimal; weight must be positive.
items.info_body: Each row describes one item that can be selected at most once.
items.info_html:
Decision variable

For every item Optees creates a binary variable x_i: 1 means selected, 0 means excluded.

Value

The value is the contribution to the objective. Optees maximizes total selected value.

Weight

The weight consumes capacity and must be an integer in the current DP solver.

resources.hint: Define one capacity for each problem dimension, such as weight, volume, time, or budget.
resources.info_body: Each resource adds an independent capacity constraint.
resources.info_html:
Constraints

For every resource r, the model enforces sum usage_{i,r} x_i <= capacity_r.

Interpretation

An item may have high value but consume too much weight, volume, or budget. A solution must satisfy all resources at the same time.

multi_domain.hint: Choose what the variable x_i means in the multi-dimensional model.

descriptions.zero_one: Each item can be selected once or excluded: x_i ∈ {0, 1}.
descriptions.bounded: Each item can be selected an integer quantity up to a maximum limit: x_i ∈ {0, ..., u_i}.
descriptions.unbounded: Each item can be selected a non-negative integer quantity, with no explicit limit beyond resources.
descriptions.fractional: Each item can be selected as a continuous quantity. Blank limit means 1; use inf for no explicit upper bound.

multi_items.hint: Enter one row per item. Resource columns state how much the item consumes if selected.
multi_items.info_body: Each item has a binary variable and one usage vector, with one amount for every resource.
multi_items.info_html:
Decision variable

x_i = 1 means selected, x_i = 0 excluded.

Usage vector

The item row contains the vector (weight usage, volume usage, ...). The selection is feasible only when total usage of selected items stays below every capacity.

formula.body: max Σ valueᵢ xᵢ subject to Σ weightᵢ xᵢ ≤ capacity and xᵢ ∈ {0, 1}. The dynamic-programming solver is exact for this 0/1 model, but pseudo-polynomial in capacity.
formula.bounded_body: max Σ valueᵢ xᵢ subject to Σ weightᵢ xᵢ ≤ capacity and xᵢ ∈ {0, 1, ..., uᵢ}. The solver tests admissible quantities for each item and reconstructs one optimal combination.
formula.unbounded_body: max Σ valueᵢ xᵢ subject to Σ weightᵢ xᵢ ≤ capacity and xᵢ ∈ {0, 1, 2, ...}. The solver uses dynamic programming while allowing the same item to be reused multiple times.
formula.fractional_body: max Σ valueᵢ xᵢ subject to Σ weightᵢ xᵢ ≤ capacity and 0 ≤ xᵢ ≤ 1. Since variables are continuous, greedy selection by value/weight density is exact.
formula.multi_dimensional_body: max Σ valueᵢ xᵢ subject to Σ usageᵢᵣ xᵢ ≤ capacityᵣ for every resource r. The domain of xᵢ depends on the choice above: binary, bounded integer, unbounded integer, or continuous fractional.
formula.info_body: Optees solves the first Knapsack implementation with an exact dynamic-programming algorithm.
formula.info_html:
State

dp[i][w] stores the best value reachable with the first i items and capacity w.

Transition

For each item, the algorithm compares excluding it with including it if it fits.

Guarantee

For integer weights and capacity, this gives a proven optimal 0/1 solution.

errors.invalid_body: Check capacity, values, weights, maximum quantities, and resource usage. Integer variants require non-negative integer weights, capacity, and quantities; fractional weight must be positive; multi-dimensional usage values must be non-negative numbers.

sol.summary: Total weight: {total_weight} / {capacity} · remaining capacity: {remaining} · selected items: {selected}

charts.legend: Blue = value, orange = weight; green outline = selected item
charts.multi_legend: Blue = value, orange = total resource usage; green outline = selected item

header.title: Linear Programming (LP)
header.description: Linear programming helps you maximize or minimize a value (like profit or cost) subject to a set of conditions. Solutions are decimal numbers, perfect for problems where resources can be divided.

import.schema_intro: The file must be a JSON object with the following structure. Use null for unbounded variables (−∞ / +∞).

example.title: LP examples
example.intro: Use these examples as small templates when you model a continuous linear optimization problem.

block1.title: Production mix
block1.body: A workshop produces chairs and tables. Let X1 be chairs and X2 be tables. If each chair earns 30 and each table earns 50, maximize z = 30 X1 + 50 X2. Capacity constraints can be 2 X1 + 4 X2 <= 80 for machine hours and X1 + X2 <= 30 for storage. Bounds X1, X2 >= 0 mean fractional production is allowed.

block2.title: Diet or blending
block2.body: A nutrition example minimizes cost while satisfying minimum nutrients. Let X1 and X2 be kilograms of two ingredients. Minimize z = 4 X1 + 7 X2 with constraints such as 3 X1 + X2 >= 12 proteins and X1 + 2 X2 >= 10 vitamins. Use >= constraints when a requirement must be at least a threshold.

block3.title: Multiple optimal solutions
block3.body: For max z = X1 + X2 with X1 + X2 <= 6 and X1, X2 >= 0, every point on the segment X1 + X2 = 6 is optimal. The solver reports z* = 6 and ranges X1 in [0, 6], X2 in [0, 6].

block4.title: 3D test case
block4.body: Try this small 3-variable model: max z = X1 + X2 + X3, subject to X1 + X2 + X3 <= 6 and X1, X2, X3 >= 0. The optimal face is a triangle: z* = 6, each variable ranges in [0, 6], and there are infinitely many optimal solutions.

problem.title: LP problem description
problem.intro: Linear programming solves optimization problems whose objective and constraints are linear functions of continuous decision variables.

block1.title: Mathematical form
block1.body: A canonical LP can be written as min or max c^T x + offset subject to A_ub x <= b_ub, A_eq x = b_eq, and lower/upper bounds on x. The vector x contains the decision variables; c contains objective coefficients; A and b encode the constraints.

block2.title: Feasible region and optimum
block2.body: The constraints define a convex polyhedron. A linear objective reaches its optimum at a face of that polyhedron: often a single vertex, sometimes an edge, a plane, or a higher-dimensional face. When the optimal face has positive dimension, the model has infinitely many optimal solutions.

block3.title: Algorithmic behavior
block3.body: Optees calls SciPy/HiGHS through linprog. Maximization models are converted to minimization by changing the sign of c. After solving, statuses are mapped to Optimal, Infeasible, Unbounded, or NotSolved, and HiGHS diagnostics are preserved for the UI.

block4.title: Optimal ranges
block4.body: After an optimum z* is found, Optees adds the equality c^T x = z* and solves auxiliary LPs min x_i and max x_i for each variable. This gives the exact interval of optimal values for each variable. Pseudocode: solve original LP; add c^T x = z*; for every i solve min x_i and max x_i.

bounds.hint: Empty = ±∞. You can type fractions (e.g., 1/2) or 'inf'.

opt.multiple: There are infinitely many optimal solutions (multiple optima with the same objective value).
opt.segment: There are infinitely many optimal solutions: all points between {A} and {B} are optimal.
opt.range: There are infinitely many optimal solutions. Optimal variable ranges: {ranges}.
opt.not_computed: Optimal range analysis was skipped for this model size.

header.title: Continuous Nonlinear Programming (NLP)
header.description: Define continuous variables, a feasible starting point, and a nonlinear scalar objective. This workflow returns a local numerical candidate, not a proof of global optimality.

import.info_body: Use schema version 1 with problem_type nonlinear_programming. Every variable needs a name and a finite initial value. Bounds are null when absent.
import.info_html:
Core fields

Use variables, objective, and optional solver_options. The objective expression is validated by the same safe parser used by the manual form.

{
  "version": "1",
  "problem_type": "nonlinear_programming",
  "variables": [{"name": "x1", "lb": null, "ub": null, "initial": 0}],
  "objective": {"sense": "min", "expression": "(x1 - 2)**2"},
  "solver_options": {"method": "BFGS", "max_iterations": 1000, "tolerance": 1e-8}
}

variables.hint: Each variable is continuous. Leave a bound blank for no limit; the initial value is required and must satisfy the bounds.

objective.hint: Write one scalar expression using the declared variable names. The supported language is mathematical and deliberately restricted.
objective.info_body: Allowed: declared variables, finite numbers, +, -, *, /, **, unary signs, abs, sin, cos, tan, exp, log, and sqrt. The expression must remain finite at every point evaluated by the solver.
objective.info_html:
Safe language

Optees parses the expression into a restricted tree. It never executes arbitrary Python.

Example

(x1 - 2)**2 + sqrt(x2**2 + 1)

Imports, attributes, comparisons, indexing, unknown names, and multi-argument functions are rejected.

solver.hint: The method follows the local geometry from the initial point. Tolerance and iteration limit control numerical termination, not global-optimality proof.
solver.bounds_required: At least one bound is present: Optees selects L-BFGS-B, the bound-aware method in this workflow.
solver.unbounded_hint: For an unbounded model, BFGS and Nelder-Mead are available local methods; L-BFGS-B also remains valid.
solver.info_body: BFGS and Nelder-Mead are used here for unbounded models. L-BFGS-B is required for box bounds. Converged means a local termination criterion was met, not that the candidate is globally best.
solver.info_html:
Methods

BFGS is a local curvature-based method. Nelder-Mead is a derivative-free simplex method. L-BFGS-B handles lower and upper bounds.

Stopping

Max iterations limits the numerical work. Tolerance controls a method-specific stopping test.

solution.title: Nonlinear Optimization Result
solution.local_notice: This result is a local numerical candidate. Its quality can depend on the method and the initial point; it is not a global-optimality certificate.

candidate.hint: Variable values returned by the selected numerical run.

trace.hint: Initial objective followed by values captured during the run. A trace describes this run only.
trace.empty: The selected run did not provide an objective trace.
